subQuestions.questionText:
BUDGETS — RELAX 'N RENT (PTY) LTD

Sihle Bhengu started Relax 'n Rent (Pty) Ltd, which rents out printers and photocopy machines. Financial year began 1 November 2021. Sihle put in no capital.

All ink and toner is bought from Ink Solution on credit; the amount varies monthly. Ink Solution is repaid:
• 60% in the month following the purchase (5% discount received)
• 25% two months following the purchase (2% discount received)
• 15% in the third month following the purchase (no discount)

Ink and toner purchased (before discount): August 2022 R10 200; September 2022 R10 800; October 2022 R11 000.

Complete the Creditor's Payment Schedule for November 2022 (the cash that will be paid to Ink Solution in November 2022).
subQuestions.memoText:
CREDITOR'S PAYMENT SCHEDULE FOR NOVEMBER 2022:

            | Ink and toner cost | November payment
August 2022 | 10 200             | 10 200 × 15% = R1 530 ✓ (third month after purchase, no discount)
September 2022 | 10 800          | 10 800 × 25% × 98% = R2 646 ✓ (two months after, 2% discount)
October 2022 | 11 000            | 11 000 × 60% × 95% = R6 270 ✓ (month after, 5% discount)
Total paid to Ink Solution in November 2022 = 1 530 + 2 646 + 6 270 = R10 446 ✓

Teaching point: A creditor's payment schedule works out the cash paid in a given month by applying each payment percentage — and the matching discount — to the purchases of the earlier months, according to how long ago each purchase was made.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Creditor's Payment Schedule

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 1.1, plus:
• Machine rental income for November 2022 will be R144 000; per-page income R114 920.
• Relax 'n Rent bought all its original machines (R1 350 000) on credit from Copy Ink Ltd on 30 October 2021: simple interest of 8% p.a. for four years (R432 000 interest in total), repaid in equal monthly instalments over 4 years (48 instalments). A debit order pays this each month.
• Sihle plans to buy new equipment on the same terms on 1 November 2022, first payment at the end of November; the November instalment on the new equipment is R26 950.
• Technician costs: the average monthly cost in the previous year was R45 600 ÷ 12; November 2022 technician costs will be 60% higher.
• Sihle runs the business from home (40 m² of a 160 m² house); the November water and electricity account for the whole house will be about R7 340; the business share is 40/160.
• Salary: Sihle Bhengu R50 000 per month.
• Salary: Mrs Bhengu (food money) R6 900 per month; in October she took only two-thirds and will take the other third (R2 300) with her November salary.
• Office supplies: R350 is used per month, replenished and paid in cash at month-end; Sihle will also donate R500 of office supplies and R14 000 cash to a school in November.
• Phone charges and WIFI: as per the previous year's monthly average.
• Bank balance at the beginning of November 2022: R379 020.

Complete the Cash Budget for November 2022, showing your calculations.
subQuestions.memoText:
CASH BUDGET OF RELAX 'N RENT FOR NOVEMBER 2022:

RECEIPTS: R258 920
• Machine rental income: R144 000 ✓
• Per page income: R114 920 ✓

PAYMENTS (do not calculate the subtotal):
• Creditors payment: Ink Solution: R10 446 ✓ (from 1.1)
• Creditors payment: Copy Ink Ltd — old equipment: (1 350 000 + 432 000) ÷ 4 ÷ 12 = R37 125 ✓✓
• Creditors payment: Copy Ink Ltd — new equipment: R26 950 ✓
• Technician costs: (45 600 ÷ 12) × 1,6 = 3 800 × 1,6 = R6 080 ✓✓
• Water and electricity: 7 340 × 40/160 = R1 835 ✓✓
• Salary: Sihle Bhengu: R50 000 ✓
• Salary: Mrs Bhengu: 6 900 + 2 300 (the third withheld from October) = R9 200 ✓✓
• Phone charges and WIFI: 21 240 ÷ 12 = R1 770 ✓
• Office supply purchases: 350 + 500 (donated supplies replaced) = R850 ✓
• Donations: R14 000 ✓ (cash donation)

Cash surplus for the month: R100 734
Balance at the beginning of the month: R379 020
Balance at the end of the month: R479 754

Teaching point: A cash budget records only cash flows for the ONE month — the instalment sale payment is (capital + total interest) ÷ number of years ÷ 12; depreciation is excluded; and only the business's apportioned share of household costs is a business payment.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Cash Budget

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 1.2. The statement from Copy Ink Ltd (for the ORIGINAL equipment) at 31 October 2022 shows: original capital R1 350 000; original instalments 48; remaining instalments 36; outstanding capital balance R1 012 500; outstanding actual contract balance (including interest) R1 336 500. Net profit for the year (Shareholders' Equity) was R436 320. Ink Solution owes R6 020 at year end.

Using the Copy Ink Ltd statement, complete the Equity and Liabilities part of the Statement of Financial Position as at 31 October 2022 (non-current liabilities, current liabilities).
subQuestions.memoText:
EXTRACT — EQUITY AND LIABILITIES AT 31 OCTOBER 2022:

Shareholder's Equity: R436 320 ✓ (net profit for the year; Sihle put in no capital)
Non-current liabilities — Copy Ink Ltd: R675 000 ✓
  Working: outstanding capital R1 012 500; the portion due within 12 months (12 instalments of R1 012 500 ÷ 36 = R28 125 each = R337 500) is a current liability, so 1 012 500 − 337 500 = R675 000 is non-current. (2/3 non-current : 1/3 current.)
Current liabilities (do not calculate the total):
• Ink Solution: R6 020 ✓
• Copy Ink Ltd: R337 500 ✓ (the capital portion due within the next 12 months)

Mark note: 1 mark for using the amount EXCLUDING interest (R1 012 500), regardless of which liability column; 1 mark for splitting 1/3 into current and 2/3 into non-current.

Teaching point: Only the CAPITAL still owed goes on the balance sheet (the future interest is not yet a liability). That capital is then split — the amount repayable within the next financial year is a current liability, the rest is non-current.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Statement of Financial Position extract

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.3.1. Name the GAAP principle that dictates which figure, from the statement from Copy Ink Ltd, you used to complete the liabilities section above.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE ✓: the matching (accrual) principle; OR fair presentation; OR historical cost.

Teaching point: Under the matching / accrual principle, interest is only recognised as a liability in the period it accrues — so only the capital owed (not the future interest) is shown as a liability now.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - GAAP principles

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 1.2. The November 2022 instalment on the NEW equipment is R26 950. It is bought on the same terms as before: paid off monthly over 4 years (48 instalments), with simple interest of 8% p.a. for four years added to the capital (total interest = 8% × 4 years = 32% of capital).

Calculate the cost (capital amount) of the new equipment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Cost of the new equipment:
Total contract value = 26 950 × 12 × 4 = R1 293 600 ✓
This includes 4 years' interest at 8% p.a. = 32% of capital, so the contract value = 132% of capital.
Capital = 1 293 600 × 100/132 = R980 000 ✓✓

Teaching point: With simple interest of 8% p.a. over 4 years, the total repaid is 132% of the capital. Divide the total contract value by 1,32 to strip the interest back out and recover the cash cost.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Instalment sale capital amount

subQuestions.questionText:
Use the same information as 1.3.1 and 1.4. After buying the new machines on 1 November 2022, Relax 'n Rent's non-current liabilities would be R675 000 (old Copy Ink Ltd) + R735 000 (the non-current portion of the new R980 000 instalment sale). Shareholders' equity is R436 320.

Calculate the debt-equity ratio for 1 November 2022 should Relax 'n Rent buy the new machines.
subQuestions.memoText:
Debt-equity ratio:
= (675 000 + 735 000) : 436 320
= 1 410 000 : 436 320 ✓✓
= 3,23 : 1 ✓

Teaching point: Debt-equity ratio = non-current liabilities : shareholders' equity. At 3,23 : 1 the business owes over three times its equity — very high gearing / financial risk.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Debt-equity ratio

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.5.1. Based on the debt-equity ratio calculated in 1.5.1, do you think that Copy Ink Ltd should sell the new equipment to Relax 'n Rent on credit?
subQuestions.memoText:
✓: No. Relax 'n Rent's debt would be roughly four times its equity — very high risk. Based on the debt-equity ratio alone, Copy Ink Ltd should NOT extend the credit.

Teaching point: A very high debt-equity ratio signals that the borrower already relies heavily on debt, raising the risk that a new lender will not be repaid.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Credit decision from gearing

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.3.1. Relax 'n Rent has a 200% return on equity. Explain why Relax 'n Rent has such a high return on shareholders' equity.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓: The return is 200% because Sihle did not put in any capital — the equity is very small (only the profit earned by the business), so even a modest profit is a huge percentage of that tiny equity base.

Teaching point: Return on equity = profit ÷ average equity. When the equity base is near zero (no capital contributed), the ratio balloons — it does not necessarily mean the business is exceptionally profitable in rand terms.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Return on equity interpretation

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 1.2. Besides the gearing, explain TWO other factors that Copy Ink Ltd should consider before granting Relax 'n Rent more credit, then advise Copy Ink Ltd whether to sell them the new equipment.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO factors + an advice ✓✓:
• Relax 'n Rent has no cash-flow problems — good liquidity and excess cash (the November cash budget shows a large surplus).
• Relax 'n Rent pays by debit order and its bank balance is healthy, so payments would not bounce — reliable payer.
• If Relax 'n Rent ever defaulted, Copy Ink Ltd could repossess the machines (an instalment sale) and recover the outstanding amount.
Advice: YES — with its strong cash flow Relax 'n Rent can easily make the payments; it is not really a credit risk, and the sale grows Copy Ink Ltd's revenue.

Teaching point: Gearing is only one lens — a lender also weighs the borrower's cash flow, payment reliability, and the security it holds (here, the equipment itself).
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Factors in a credit decision

subQuestions.questionText: Sihle suspects that one of the technicians is charging him for going out to businesses to service or fix machines but is not actually going there — charging for jobs he did not do. Discuss a control measure Sihle can implement to stop this from happening.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓: Require the technician to complete a job card for every call-out, recording what was done, the date and the time, which the client must stamp or sign to confirm the visit. Job cards must be handed in before the technician is paid.

Teaching point: Requiring independent, client-verified documentation before payment is a standard control against billing for work not performed.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Internal control over contractors

subQuestions.questionText: Sihle has hired you as an external auditor. Explain in detail why you would allow, or not allow, Mrs Bhengu's salary (R6 900 per month, the household food money) to remain in the Statement of Comprehensive Income. Mrs Bhengu does not work for the business.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓: NO — it may not remain. Mrs Bhengu does not work for the business, so her 'salary' is not a business expense; it is Sihle's private household spending. Recording it as a salary to reduce the company's tax is unethical and amounts to tax evasion, which is illegal. (An answer that says 'yes, allow it' earns no marks because it is illegal.)

Teaching point: Only genuine business expenses may appear in the financial statements; dressing up private drawings as a salary to lower tax is tax evasion.
subQuestions.topic: Budgets - Ethics and the external auditor

subQuestions.questionText:
COMPANY ANALYSIS — ITALTILE LIMITED (retailer and manufacturer of tiles, bathroom ware and related products; extensive property portfolio; controlling interests in importers and manufacturers).

In its financial statements Italtile published a seven-year review (2015–2021). Discuss the value of this compared with just showing the latest two years.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid points ✓✓:
• It shows trends and consistency over time.
• It shows the overall performance across seven years rather than just the current years, where an event like lockdown, looting or something out of the ordinary may have distorted a single year.

Teaching point: A multi-year review lets users separate a genuine long-term trend from a one-off good or bad year.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Value of a multi-year review

subQuestions.questionText:
Seven-year review (mark-up): 2015 63%; 2016 67%; 2017 68%; 2018 62%; 2019 60%; 2020 61%; 2021 79%.

Explain why the mark-up fluctuates from year to year.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid reason ✓✓:
• Italtile runs sales (at reduced mark-up) to clear end-of-range products, and the volume of these clearance sales differs from year to year.
• A change in demand for the products (customers willing to pay more or less).

Teaching point: The reported mark-up is a blended figure; the mix of full-price versus discounted/clearance sales moves it up and down between years.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Explaining a fluctuating mark-up

subQuestions.questionText:
Seven-year review: Turnover 2020 R6 690m → 2021 R9 135m; Cost of sales 2020 R4 145m → 2021 R5 106m; Mark-up 2020 61% → 2021 79%.

Discuss whether the directors would be pleased with the 2021 gross profit and mark-up. Motivate with TWO calculations.
subQuestions.memoText:
The directors should be very pleased ✓. Motivation with two calculations ✓✓✓:
• Mark-up rose from 61% to 79% — an 18 percentage-point increase (or (79 − 61) ÷ 61 × 100 ≈ 29,5% higher).
• At the same time sales grew: turnover up (9 135 − 6 690) ÷ 6 690 × 100 = 34,76%, and cost of sales up (5 106 − 4 145) ÷ 4 145 × 100 ≈ 23,2% — so they sold MORE units AND at a higher margin.

Teaching point: A higher mark-up is only unambiguously good if volumes hold up; here both the margin and the sales volume increased, which is the ideal outcome.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Gross profit and mark-up

subQuestions.questionText:
Seven-year review: Gross profit 2015 R1 204m, Operating profit 2015 R905m; Gross profit 2021 R4 029m, Operating profit 2021 R2 554m.

Comment on whether Italtile's operating expenses are being well controlled. (Yes/No — the explanation earns the marks.)
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid analysis ✓✓✓:
• The gap between gross profit and operating profit was (1 204 − 905) ÷ 1 204 = 24,8% of gross profit in 2015; in 2021 it was (4 029 − 2 554) ÷ 4 029 = 36,6%. So proportionally MORE of the gross profit is being consumed by operating expenses than before — they will need to make sure this does not keep rising.
• In rand terms the gap grew from R299m to R1 475m — a 393% increase, far above inflation.
• However, the higher operating expenses can be justified because they went hand in hand with a much higher turnover.

Teaching point: Expense control is judged by the operating expenses as a proportion of gross profit (or sales) over time, and by whether extra spending actually generated extra revenue.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Expense control

subQuestions.questionText: Italtile has an extensive property portfolio. Discuss TWO detailed advantages for Italtile of owning most of the property on which its shops and distribution facilities are built.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO detailed advantages ✓✓✓✓ (2 marks each):
• Property costs per m² are generally cheaper than rent over time; rent keeps rising, whereas loan interest falls as the loan is repaid.
• Displaying tiles, bathroom ware and heavy stock needs a lot of space; owning the land lets Italtile build showrooms and storerooms the right size, with loading areas for forklifts.
• Land and buildings add value to the financial position and generally appreciate over time, making the balance sheet more stable and valuable.

Teaching point: Owning trading property converts an ever-rising rental expense into a depreciating/appreciating asset and gives the retailer control over the layout it needs.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Owning versus renting property

subQuestions.questionText:
The 2020 Statement of Financial Position has four missing figures (A, B, C, D). Use the financial ratios to calculate them (do NOT calculate the '?' figures). Show your calculations.

Known 2020 figures (Rm): Inventories R897; Cash and cash equivalents R860; Equity R5 630; Current ratio 3,35 : 1; Acid test ratio 2,2 : 1; Debt-equity ratio 0,2 : 1.
• A = Current liabilities
• B = Current assets
• C = Trade and other receivables
• D = Non-current liabilities
subQuestions.memoText:
A (Current liabilities): the acid test excludes inventory, so (current assets − 897) ÷ A = 2,2 and current assets ÷ A = 3,35. Subtracting: 897 ÷ A = 3,35 − 2,2 = 1,15 → A = 897 ÷ 1,15 = R780m ✓✓

B (Current assets): B = A × 3,35 = 780 × 3,35 = R2 613m ✓✓

C (Trade and other receivables): C = B − Inventories − Cash = 2 613 − 897 − 860 = R856m ✓✓

D (Non-current liabilities): debt-equity ratio 0,2 : 1, so D = 5 630 × 0,2 = R1 126m ✓✓

Teaching point: The current and acid-test ratios share the same denominator (current liabilities); subtracting one from the other isolates inventory ÷ current liabilities, which unlocks the whole current section.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Back-calculating from ratios

subQuestions.questionText:
Cost of sales 2021 R5 106m; Inventories 2021 R1 164m; Inventories 2020 R897m.

Calculate the stock turnover rate for 2021, then write a detailed comment on whether this would be a satisfactory rate for Italtile.
subQuestions.memoText:
Stock turnover rate (2021):
= 5 106 ÷ [(1 164 + 897) ÷ 2]
= 5 106 ÷ 1 030,5
= 4,95 times ✓✓✓

Comment ✓: 4,95 times is an excellent stock turnover rate for products such as tiles and bathroom ware, which take years to go out of date and do not perish — the business is not holding stock unnecessarily long.

Teaching point: Stock turnover rate = cost of sales ÷ average inventory. What counts as 'good' depends on the product; for slow-moving, non-perishable homeware, turning stock roughly five times a year is strong.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Stock turnover rate

subQuestions.questionText: The current ratio has dropped from 4,6 : 1 in 2019 to 2,28 : 1 in 2021. The debtors collection period improved from 44 days (2019) to 32 days (2021) and the stock turnover rate also improved. Explain, with a reason, whether this drop is an improvement or not.
subQuestions.memoText:
It is an IMPROVEMENT ✓✓✓:
• The current ratio is a balance between current assets and current liabilities. At 4,6 : 1 too much cash was tied up in current assets (or too little was being bought on credit, or creditors were being paid off too fast). Dropping to 2,28 : 1 means current assets and current liabilities are now more in balance.
• At the same time the debtors' collection period and the stock turnover rate improved, and more is being bought on credit — all signs that liquidity is being managed better, not worse.

Teaching point: A very high current ratio is not automatically good — it can mean idle resources. A fall towards the 2 : 1 benchmark, alongside faster collections and stock turnover, is a sign of tighter working-capital management.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Interpreting a falling current ratio

subQuestions.questionText:
Seven-year review — Cash flows from/utilised in (Rm), for the year ended 30 June:
• operating activities: 2021 R1 397; ... 2015 R443
• investing activities: 2021 (R947); ... 2015 (R175)
• financing activities: 2021 R1 081; ... 2015 R392

Analyse the cash flow movement shown in the seven-year review, and explain whether this is a good or bad way of handling their cash.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓ (where cash comes from) ✓ (where it goes) ✓ (that this is good):
• Italtile generates the majority of its cash from operating activities and from financing activities (raising capital / loans).
• That cash is used in investing activities (consistently negative), i.e. buying property and long-term assets that will grow the business.
• This is a GOOD pattern — a healthy company funds its expansion from operations and financing and ploughs it into productive assets.

Teaching point: The classic 'healthy' cash-flow shape is positive operating, negative investing (growing), and financing that supports growth — cash earned is reinvested rather than merely propping up operations.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Cash flow pattern

subQuestions.questionText: Use the case study on Italtile. Write down TWO examples of the investing activities that Italtile has that were mentioned in the case study.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO ✓✓:
• Buying property (the extensive property portfolio).
• Buying / holding a controlling interest in related companies (importers, manufacturers).
• Investing in financial investments.

Teaching point: Investing activities are cash spent acquiring long-term assets and investments — for Italtile, property and stakes in group companies.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Identifying investing activities

subQuestions.questionText:
Profit before 28% taxation 2021: R2 555m. Equity: 2021 R6 713m; 2020 R5 630m. Return on shareholders' equity: 2020 17,6%; 2019 23,0%.

Calculate the return on shareholders' equity for 2021, and then comment on whether the directors of Italtile would be happy with the return.
subQuestions.memoText:
Return on shareholders' equity (2021):
= [2 555 × 72/100] ÷ [(6 713 + 5 630) ÷ 2] × 100
= 1 839,60 ÷ 6 171,50 × 100
= 29,81% ✓✓✓

Comment ✓: Yes, they should be happy — the return is up from 23,0% in 2019 (recovered from the effects of lockdown) and is far higher than the return available on an alternative investment (e.g. a fixed deposit).

Teaching point: ROSHE uses profit AFTER tax (here 72% of profit before tax) over average equity; it is judged against the prior years and against the risk-free return an investor could otherwise earn.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Return on shareholders' equity

subQuestions.questionText:
Earnings per share 2021: 141 cents. Dividends per share 2021: 106 cents. Net asset value 2021: 522 cents. Return on shareholders' equity 2021 ≈ 29,81% (from 2.7.1).

Although the EPS was 141 cents, the DPS was only 106 cents. Discuss whether the shareholders would be pleased with the 106 cents, or whether they should have received a DPS of 141 cents.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓: Shareholders should be pleased with 106 cents.
• Italtile paid out about 75% of its earnings as dividends (106 ÷ 141) and retained 25% to build the company's value.
• 75% of a strong ~30% return is an excellent dividend; retaining 25% is a sound decision for future growth, which will benefit shareholders through a rising share price / NAV.

Teaching point: Paying out every cent of earnings leaves nothing to reinvest; a high payout ratio combined with some retention is generally the mark of a well-run, growing company.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Dividend payout policy

subQuestions.questionText:
Net asset value 2021: 522 cents. Closing share price at year end 2021: 1 667 cents.

Explain what the Net Asset Value represents and why the share price is so much higher than it.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓:
• The Net Asset Value represents the book value of a share — ordinary shareholders' equity divided by the number of shares in issue.
• The market share price (1 667 cents) is far above the book value (522 cents) because investors want the share — they believe Italtile is a good investment and expect strong future earnings and growth, so they are willing to pay well above net asset value.

Teaching point: NAV is a backward-looking book figure; the market price reflects investors' expectations of FUTURE performance, so a well-regarded growth company trades at a large premium to NAV.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - NAV versus market price

subQuestions.questionText:
Extract from the auditor's report: 'We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion.'

What is the purpose of the external auditor's report?
subQuestions.memoText:
✓: To let the shareholders know whether the financial statements are reliable (a fair presentation they can depend on).

Teaching point: The external audit report gives shareholders independent assurance that the directors' financial statements can be trusted.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Purpose of the audit report

subQuestions.questionText: Write down TWO pieces of audit evidence the external auditors would obtain to verify the water and electricity amount in the Statement of Comprehensive Income.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO ✓✓:
• Take a sample of the municipal invoices / statements for water and electricity.
• Inspect the Cash Payments Journal and the bank statement to confirm the amounts were actually paid.
• Follow the process to check that the CPJ entries were posted correctly to the ledger and the trial balance.

Teaching point: Audit evidence for an expense is traced through the full cycle — source document (municipal bill), payment record (CPJ / bank statement), and correct posting to the ledger.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Gathering audit evidence

subQuestions.questionText:
Extract from the Corporate Governance report: Italtile offers an Employee Wellness Programme giving staff access to financial consultants (budgeting, saving, debt counselling, wills, home loans, insurance, tax). Italtile may NOT count this as a corporate social responsibility (CSR) programme because, by law, CSR programmes may not benefit the company's own employees or their families.

Explain the difference between Corporate Governance and a Corporate Social Responsibility programme. Then discuss whether Italtile should be spending time and effort on the Employee Wellness Programme even though it does not count towards CSR.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓ (any of the following combined into a short answer):
• Corporate Governance is the ethical management of the company itself; CSR is what the company does to help the environment and the community AROUND it.
• Italtile SHOULD still run the programme — it is ethical management towards its own employees.
• On average about seven people in South Africa depend on one employed person, so a financially secure workforce benefits many families and the wider community; staff also work better when they feel cared for and have fewer money worries.

Teaching point: Good governance includes looking after employees even when the spending earns no CSR 'credit'; the social benefit still flows through to families and the community.
subQuestions.topic: Company Analysis - Corporate governance vs CSR

subQuestions.questionText:
RECONCILIATIONS — DAZZLING DESIGNS (decorates shopping centres and shops for occasions; owned by Jemma). Corporate clients have accounts; other customers pay half upfront and half on collection.

Explain the importance of a Debtors' Age Analysis.
subQuestions.memoText:
✓✓: It is used as a control mechanism to track how promptly each debtor is paying, so that corrective action (reminders, withholding further service, handing over) can be taken when payments are not made on time.

Teaching point: An age analysis groups each debtor's balance by how overdue it is, flagging slow payers before the debt becomes uncollectable.
subQuestions.topic: Debtors Reconciliation - Purpose of an age analysis

subQuestions.questionText:
Debtors' Age Analysis drawn up on 31 October 2022:
120+ days: R16 000 | 90 days: R3 500 | 60 days: R89 400 | 30 days: R120 350 | Current: R92 680

Errors discovered after statements were sent:
1. The R16 000 in 120+ days (a Santa's sled damaged in MegaSpend Mall) is to be written off.
2. Coffee Break was granted a 20% discount for paying in September but the discount (on an invoice originally R36 600, dated 5 August in the '60 days' column) was not recorded — they paid R29 280; the R7 320 discount must be removed from the 60-day column.
3. Beachside Mall paid R20 000 on 29 October (not recorded), applied to: 10 October invoice R18 700 (30-day column, so −R13 000... see memo), 31 August invoice R12 800 (60-day column), 15 July invoice R2 300.
4. An invoice for R25 300 dated 2 October (30-day column) was omitted.
5. A credit note for R13 000 dated 3 October (30-day column) was omitted.

Make the corrections to the Debtors' Age Analysis (it does not need to be totalled).
subQuestions.memoText:
CORRECTIONS TO THE DEBTORS' AGE ANALYSIS:

120+ days: 16 000 − 16 000 (write-off, error 1) ✓
90 days: 3 500 − 2 300 (Beachside Mall payment allocated to the 15 July invoice, error 3) ✓
60 days: 89 400 − 12 800 (Beachside Mall payment to the 31 Aug invoice, error 3) − 7 320 (Coffee Break discount not recorded, error 2) ✓✓
30 days: 120 350 − 13 000 (credit note omitted, error 5; and the balance of the Beachside Mall R20 000 payment) ✓
Current: 92 680 − 4 900 (remainder of Beachside Mall payment against the 10 Oct invoice) + 25 300 (invoice omitted, error 4) ✓

(Beachside Mall's R20 000 clears R2 300 + R12 800 first, leaving R4 900 against the R18 700 October invoice.)

Teaching point: Each correction moves an amount into the correct ageing bucket — payments clear the OLDEST debt first, write-offs and unrecorded discounts reduce the relevant column, and omitted invoices/credit notes are added or subtracted in the month of their date.
subQuestions.topic: Debtors Reconciliation - Correcting an age analysis

subQuestions.questionText: In error 1, a Santa's sled was damaged by children in MegaSpend Mall and this caused a dispute between Dazzling Designs and the mall over who should pay. Jemma realises the same thing could happen at any mall they decorate. Discuss what she can do to prevent this from becoming an issue in the future.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any valid preventative measures ✓✓✓:
• Take out insurance on the large, expensive decorations.
• Include a clause in the contract that the client is liable for any damage / repair costs.
• Require a security deposit that is only refunded once the equipment is returned undamaged; repairs are deducted from the deposit.
• Set up the big, expensive decorations near where mall security is stationed.

Teaching point: Risk of damage to assets on a client's premises is managed contractually (liability clauses, deposits), by insurance, or by physical safeguards.
subQuestions.topic: Debtors Reconciliation - Managing risk of asset damage

subQuestions.questionText: Some of Dazzling Designs' repeat cash customers are asking to open accounts. Discuss ONE reason as to whether Jemma should allow them to open accounts or not.
subQuestions.memoText:
Either view is accepted with a valid reason ✓:
Yes — they may spend more; they are repeat customers so you know they pay; you know where they are based.
No — it adds admin to track them; they already hire Dazzling Designs without credit, so keep it that way; bigger risk of bad debts; more risk of cash-flow problems.

Teaching point: Offering credit can grow sales but adds administration, bad-debt risk and a cash-flow lag — the trade-off depends on how well the customer is known.
subQuestions.topic: Debtors Reconciliation - Whether to grant credit

subQuestions.questionText: Use the same information as 3.4.1. If Dazzling Designs were to open accounts for these customers, write down THREE terms and conditions that Dazzling Designs should put in their contracts.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any THREE ✓✓✓:
• The customer must agree to a credit check.
• How long they have to pay (the payment terms).
• Penalties (interest) if they do not pay on time.
• A discount for early payment.
• They may not book another event until the previous one is paid for.

Teaching point: Credit terms should set out the vetting, the payment period, the consequences of late payment, and the incentive for early payment.
subQuestions.topic: Debtors Reconciliation - Credit terms and conditions

subQuestions.questionText:
Dazzling Designs received a statement from its creditor Authentic Wood showing a balance of R106 810 at 31 October 2022. The Creditors' Ledger account of Authentic Wood in Dazzling Designs' books shows a different balance.

Additional information:
• Credit note 08 (R8 200 on the statement) was recorded incorrectly by Authentic Wood; Dazzling Designs' debit note 16 was for R8 500 — the statement must be reduced by R300.
• Invoice D53 for R15 960 was issued to Ditzy Design, not Dazzling Designs — remove it from the statement.
• The interest on 1 October must decrease by R18 because of the credit-note mistake.
• The EFT of R47 300 on 30 October had not yet reflected on Authentic Wood's statement.

Complete the Creditor's Reconciliation Statement.
subQuestions.memoText:
CREDITOR'S RECONCILIATION STATEMENT (Do not calculate the total):
Incorrect balance (per statement): R106 810
• Credit note 08 (recorded R8 200 instead of R8 500): (R300) ✓
• Invoice D53 (issued to Ditzy Design, not us): (R15 960) ✓
• Interest (overstated by R18): (R18) ✓
• EFT paid 30 October, not yet on the statement: (R47 300) ✓
Corrected balance: DO NOT CALCULATE

Teaching point: The reconciliation statement adjusts the SUPPLIER'S balance for the supplier's errors (wrong credit note, wrong interest, an invoice that belongs to another customer) and for a payment in transit that the supplier has not yet recorded.
subQuestions.topic: Creditors Reconciliation - Reconciliation statement
